targets.title: Peer-to-Peer Communication Across Network Address Translators
targets.authors: Bryan Ford, Pyda Srisuresh, Dan Kegel
targets.venue: USENIX Annual Technical Conference, General Track
targets.why_needed: Original description of UDP and TCP hole punching as a mechanism: two peers behind independent NATs each send to the other's externally observed address, opening a path through their own translator without any special NAT-side support. Every later hole-punching measurement (Halkes/Pouwelse 2011, Trautwein et al. 2025-26) states its success rate against this mechanism definition.

targets.title: STUN - Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Through Network Address Translators (NATs)
targets.authors: Jonathan Rosenberg, Joel Weinberger, Christian Huitema, Rohan Mahy
targets.why_needed: Defines the four-way NAT behavior classification (full cone, restricted cone, port-restricted cone, symmetric) that every later prevalence measurement in this domain reports its percentages against. A symmetric NAT assigns a different external port per destination address, which is the behavior that defeats hole punching and forces relay fallback.

targets.title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
targets.authors: Marc Petit-Huguenin, Gonzalo Salgueiro, Jonathan Rosenberg, Dan Wing, Rohan Mahy, Philip Matthews
targets.venue: IETF RFC 8489 (obsoletes RFC 5389, itself obsoleting RFC 3489's protocol machinery)
targets.why_needed: Current STUN specification: the binding-request mechanism a client uses to learn its own server-reflexive (public) address and port, which every hole-punching and ICE candidate-gathering procedure depends on for its first step.

targets.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
targets.authors: Tirumaleswar Reddy, Alan Johnston, Philip Matthews, Jonathan Rosenberg
targets.why_needed: Defines the relay-fallback mechanism: a client allocates a public transport address on a third-party server and every packet to and from the peer transits that server. This is the cost baseline against which any direct-connection success rate (hole punching, DCUtR) is measured, because every failed direct attempt falls back to this.

targets.title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal
targets.authors: Ari Keränen, Christer Holmberg, Jonathan Rosenberg
targets.why_needed: Defines candidate gathering (host, server-reflexive via STUN, relayed via TURN), connectivity checks between every candidate pair, and the priority formula that selects among simultaneously viable paths. This is the procedure WebRTC and every browser peer connection runs to decide whether a direct path or a relay is used, and it is the object of the recent QUIC-multiplexing and lightweight-signaling proposals below.

targets.title: UDP NAT and Firewall Puncturing in the Wild
targets.authors: Gertjan P. Halkes, Johan A. Pouwelse
targets.why_needed: Earliest large-scale in-network measurement of hole-punching success on a production P2P system (the Tribler/IPv8 network at TU Delft), predating the 2025-26 DCUtR study by 14 years. Establishes the historical baseline for what fraction of peers sit behind a NAT type that allows puncturing and what fraction of attempts between them succeed, which the newer DCUtR figures must be read against as a before/after comparison rather than in isolation.

targets.title: Mass Adoption of NATs: Survey and experiments on carrier-grade NATs
targets.authors: Orestis Kanaris, Johan Pouwelse
targets.why_needed: The 2023-or-later survey this domain requires. Covers carrier-grade NAT (CGN) deployment specifically, run by the same TU Delft group as the 2011 hole-punching baseline, so it is positioned to state what changed for P2P reachability between 2011 and 2023 on the operator side rather than the client side.

targets.title: An Untold Story of Middleboxes in Cellular Networks
targets.authors: Zhaoguang Wang, Zhiyun Qian, Qiang Xu, Zhuoqing Morley Mao, Ming Zhang
targets.why_needed: Direct, controlled measurement of NAT and firewall behavior across carriers, distinguishing mapping type (endpoint-independent/full-cone vs. endpoint-dependent/symmetric) from filtering type and from binding timeout, on cellular networks specifically. This is the primary source the domain's cellular-symmetric-NAT prevalence figures must be checked against rather than restated from a secondary blog summary.

targets.title: A Multi-perspective Analysis of Carrier-Grade NAT Deployment
targets.authors: Philipp Richter, Florian Wohlfart, Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, Mark Allman, Randy Bush, Anja Feldmann, Christian Kreibich, Nicholas Weaver, Vern Paxson
targets.why_needed: Multi-vantage-point (traceroute, BISmark home-router, and Netalyzr client-side) measurement of how many access networks interpose carrier-grade NAT between a residential subscriber and the public Internet, i.e. how often a subscriber has no directly assignable public address at all regardless of what their own equipment does. Bounds the ceiling on end-to-end direct reachability independent of the two peers' own hole-punching behavior.

targets.title: Inferring Carrier-Grade NAT Deployment in the Wild
targets.authors: Ioana Livadariu, Karyn Benson, Ahmed Elmokashfi, Amogh Dhamdhere, Alberto Dainotti
targets.why_needed: A second, methodologically distinct (large-scale active-probing rather than vantage-point-limited) measurement of carrier-grade NAT prevalence, two years after Richter et al. Needed as the comparison figure to check whether the 2016 estimate held, rose, or fell, and to check which measurement technique the numbers used in synthesis should cite as closer to a global figure.

targets.title: Large-Scale Measurement of NAT Traversal for the Decentralized Web: A Case Study of DCUtR in IPFS
targets.authors: Dennis Trautwein, Cornelius Ihle, Moritz Schubotz, Corinna Breitinger, Bela Gipp
targets.venue: arXiv preprint (CoRR); DOI registered for a forthcoming ACM venue but not yet resolving as of retrieval; an earlier four-author preprint titled "Challenging Tribal Knowledge -- Large Scale Measurement Campaign on Decentralized NAT Traversal" (arXiv 2510.27500, Oct. 2025) is the same underlying study
targets.why_needed: The measurement this domain is defined around. First large-scale, longitudinal measurement of the Direct Connection Upgrade through Relay (DCUtR) hole-punching protocol on a production libp2p network (IPFS): 4.4 million traversal attempts, 85,000+ networks, 167 countries. Reports a hole-punching-stage success rate of 70% +/- 7.1% CONDITIONAL on prerequisite relay reservation and public-address discovery already having succeeded (the published-version abstract's own wording, which corrects the unconditional framing an earlier draft implied), TCP and QUIC statistically indistinguishable at ~70%, success independent of which relay coordinated the attempt, and 97.6% of successes completing on the first attempt. The conditioning clause is load-bearing: this is not the fraction of all connection attempts that reach a direct path, only the fraction of the already-relay-connected subset that then upgrades.

targets.title: Beware: NAT Traversal is a Simple and Efficient Approach to Open Firewall Holes
targets.authors: Elias P. Duarte Jr., Kleber V. Cardoso, Micael O. M. C. de Mello, João G. G. Borges
targets.why_needed: States hole punching as an exploitable primitive: an attacker who controls one endpoint of a coordinated punch can use the technique to induce a NAT or stateful firewall to accept inbound packets on a port it would otherwise drop, independent of any P2P application's own intent. This is the security exposure that a direct-reachability design has to weigh against the connectivity gain, stated as a mechanism and a failure condition rather than as a value judgment about whether to use hole punching at all.

targets.title: The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment
targets.authors: Adam Langley, Alistair Riddoch, Alyssa Wilk, Antonio Vicente, Charles Krasic, Dan Zhang, Fan Yang, Fedor Kouranov, Ian Swett, Janardhan Iyengar, Jeff Bailey, Jeremy Dorfman, Jim Roskind, Joanna Kulik, Patrik Westin, Raman Tenneti, Robbie Shade, Ryan Hamilton, Victor Vasiliev, Wan-Teh Chang, Zhongyi Shi
targets.why_needed: Defines QUIC: a transport multiplexed over UDP with a 0- or 1-round-trip handshake combining transport and cryptographic setup, per-stream flow control avoiding head-of-line blocking across streams, and connection IDs that let a connection survive a change of IP address or port (a NAT rebinding, or a client moving from Wi-Fi to cellular) without a new handshake. The connection-ID-based migration mechanism is the property every later QUIC-for-NAT-traversal proposal in this domain builds on.

targets.title: Taking a Long Look at QUIC: An Approach for Rigorous Evaluation of Rapidly Evolving Transport Protocols
targets.authors: Arash Molavi Kakhki, Samuel Jero, David Choffnes, Cristina Nita-Rotaru, Alan Mislove
targets.venue: ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC); journal version in Communications of the ACM, 2019
targets.why_needed: Independent, controlled comparison of QUIC against TCP+TLS across a matrix of emulated network conditions (packet loss, latency) rather than QUIC's own designers' benchmarks. Needed as the comparison-side numbers for any claim that QUIC outperforms TCP for a peer-to-peer transport, and as a caution that a rapidly evolving protocol's measured advantage in one snapshot version may not hold in a later one, which the IMC 2024 replication below tests directly.

targets.title: Replication: "Taking a long look at QUIC"
targets.authors: Naveenraj Muthuraj, Nooshin Eghbal, Paul Lu
targets.why_needed: Re-runs the Kakhki et al. 2017 QUIC-vs-TCP comparison seven years later against the now-standardized IETF QUIC (RFC 9000) rather than Google's pre-standard GQUIC. Directly tests whether the 2017 comparison still holds after the protocol changed, which is exactly the forward-mining check this domain's brief requires before any 2017 QUIC performance number is carried into a 2026 architecture.

targets.title: Implementing NAT Hole Punching with QUIC
targets.authors: Jinyu Liang, Wei Xu, Taotao Wang, Qing Yang, Shengli Zhang
targets.why_needed: Proposes and measures a QUIC-based hole-punching scheme as a direct alternative to TCP-based hole punching, reporting reduced punching time in weak-network conditions, and separately measures reconnection cost after a punched path breaks (from a network transition or a NAT binding timeout): QUIC connection migration restores the path 2 round trips faster than QUIC re-punching and 3 round trips faster than TCP re-punching. This is a transport property (connection migration) avoiding repetition of the NAT-traversal procedure rather than a faster way to repeat it.

targets.title: An Analysis of QUIC Connection Migration in the Wild
targets.authors: Aurélien Buchet, Cristel Pelsser
targets.why_needed: Internet-wide active scan measuring what fraction of deployed QUIC servers actually support the connection-migration mechanism the QUIC specification defines and that the NAT-traversal proposals above depend on, as opposed to what the specification permits in principle. Needed because a migration-dependent NAT-resilience design is only as good as server-side deployment of the feature, and this paper states that some of the most-visited destinations do not yet support it.

targets.title: QUIC as Multiplexing Layer in WebRTC
targets.authors: Mathis Engelbart, Fabian Willi Fromwald, Jörg Ott
targets.why_needed: Proposes replacing WebRTC's separate DTLS/SCTP data-channel stack and SRTP media stack with a single QUIC connection carrying both, removing one of the two independent NAT-traversal and encryption handshakes a browser peer connection currently runs. Directly answers the domain question of what a browser tab's transport stack can be simplified to, as opposed to what it is today.

targets.title: Lightweight Call Signaling and Peer-to-Peer Control of WebRTC Video Conferencing
targets.authors: Kundan Singh
targets.why_needed: Describes and implements a multiparty WebRTC application with no media server: signaling piggybacks on existing push notifications or on email, and conference control and data storage run over a peer-to-peer network of the browser clients themselves using WebRTC data channels. States what a set of browser tabs, with no server in the data path and only a minimal signaling channel, can be made to do as a self-organizing network.

targets.title: rtc_peer_connection.cc: kMaxPeerConnections limit enforced by RTCPeerConnection construction
targets.authors: Chromium project (Blink renderer, third_party/blink/renderer/modules/peerconnection)
targets.why_needed: Primary-source (source code, read directly, not a snippet) statement of a browser tab's hard connection ceiling: the constant kMaxPeerConnections = 500 is checked at every RTCPeerConnection construction, and construction past the limit throws rather than degrading. This is a concrete, versioned bound on what a browser tab can do as a network participant, not a claim about it.

targets.title: Circuit Relay v2 (libp2p specification)
targets.authors: Dimitris Vyzovitis (@vyzo), with interest-group review by Max Inden, Steven Allen, Raúl Kripalani
targets.venue: libp2p/specs repository, recommendation-stage specification, revision r3
targets.why_needed: Defines the store-and-forward relay mechanism DCUtR (Trautwein et al., above) upgrades away from when direct connectivity succeeds: a relay accepts a bounded, time-limited, data-capped reservation from a private peer and forwards a limited-duration circuit to it, so a public peer can serve as a relay without unbounded resource exposure. This is the relay-fallback cost structure (reservation duration default, per-relay concurrent-reservation cap, per-circuit data cap) that any relay-based fallback cost figure in this domain must be stated against, replacing circuit-relay v1's unreserved, uncapped resource use.

targets.title: Rewarding relays for decentralised NAT traversal using smart contracts
targets.authors: Navin V. Keizer, Onur Ascigil, Ioannis Psaras, George Pavlou
targets.venue: ACM International Symposium on Theory, Algorithmic Foundations, and Protocol Design for Mobile Networks and Mobile Computing (MobiHoc)
targets.why_needed: Addresses relay-fallback cost from the supplier side: relaying every packet for a symmetric-NAT peer consumes the relay operator's own bandwidth with no protocol-level return, so this paper measures a smart-contract-mediated payment mechanism intended to recruit relay capacity. Extract the measured relay bandwidth cost and the participation-rate effect of the reward mechanism as fact; the payment design itself is one candidate mechanism among others for solving the same supply problem, not a settled requirement.

targets.title: POST: A Secure, Resilient, Cooperative Messaging System
targets.authors: Alan Mislove, Ansley Post, Charles Reis, Paul Willmann, Peter Druschel, Dan S. Wallach, Xavier Bonnaire, Pierre Sens, Jean-Michel Busca, Luciana Bezerra Arantes
targets.venue: USENIX Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS)
targets.why_needed: Store-and-forward relay design for a recipient who is not currently reachable: each user's messages are stored redundantly across a set of nodes selected by a structured overlay (Pastry) rather than at a single mailbox server, and delivery to an offline recipient completes when that recipient's client next contacts any node holding a replica. This is the foundational design point for store-and-forward relaying in a decentralized setting, predating and structurally distinct from the mobile-push-plus-central-relay pattern used by today's platform-dependent messaging apps.

targets.title: Measuring IPv6 Adoption
targets.authors: Jakub Czyz, Mark Allman, Jing Zhang, Scott Iekel-Johnson, Eric Osterweil, Michael Bailey
targets.why_needed: Multi-vantage-point (traffic, routing, DNS, active-probing) measurement establishing the earlier baseline of global IPv6 adoption that the 2025-26 measurements below report growth against. Needed for a before/after comparison rather than treating a single recent number as if adoption had always been at that level.

targets.title: Measuring the Deployment of IPv6: Topology, Routing and Performance
targets.authors: Amogh Dhamdhere, Matthew Luckie, Bradley Huffaker, kc claffy, Ahmed Elmokashfi, Emile Aben
targets.why_needed: Earlier still IPv6 deployment measurement, covering AS-level topology and routing in addition to adoption share, giving a three-point (2012, 2014, 2025-26) trend for how directly reachable a dual-stack or IPv6-only peer has become over the period this domain must design for.

targets.title: Measuring NAT64 Usage in the Wild
targets.authors: Elizabeth Boswell, Stephen McQuistin, Colin Perkins, Stephen Strowes
targets.why_needed: NAT64 translates between an IPv6-only client network and IPv4-only destinations, which is a second, structurally different address-translation layer from consumer/carrier-grade NAT44 and imposes its own reachability constraint on a peer trying to be dialable: an IPv6-only host behind NAT64 cannot receive an unsolicited inbound connection from an IPv4-only peer at all without a translator-side mapping. States how widely NAT64 is deployed and under what conditions, which any IPv6-first reachability design has to account for as a still-present, not disappearing, translation boundary.

targets.title: Revisiting and Expanding the IPv6 Network Periphery: Global-Scale Measurement and Security Analysis
targets.authors: Zixuan Xie, Zitao Yang, Shurui Fang, Zhaoyang Li, Wenxing Xie, Nannan Fu, Liangyu Dong, Xiang Li
targets.why_needed: Global-scale active scan (73 countries/regions) identifying over 281.9 million active IPv6 network-periphery devices, a direct measurement of how many end-host addresses are live and probeable at the network edge rather than merely how many prefixes are routed. This is the device-level reachability count the domain's IPv6-direct-connectivity claims need, as distinct from AS-level or prefix-level adoption statistics.

targets.title: Towards a Non-Binary View of IPv6 Adoption
targets.authors: Sulyab Thottungal Valapu, John Heidemann
targets.why_needed: Argues and measures that IPv6 capability is not a single yes/no property per user or service: client-side IPv6 traffic share varies with a standard deviation over 15% across users and across days for the same user, and only 12.6% of the top 100,000 websites are fully IPv6-ready end to end (as opposed to partially, through IPv4-only dependencies). A design that assumes 'the client has IPv6' or 'the destination has IPv6' as a fixed property, rather than a fluctuating one, is checked against this paper's own measured variance.

targets.title: 3 W's of smartphone power consumption: Who, Where and How much is draining my battery?
targets.authors: Agrim Gupta, Adel Heidari, Avyakta Kalipattapu, Ish Kumar Jain, Dinesh Bharadia
targets.venue: ACM International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom)
targets.why_needed: Per-component power measurement (using on-device power measurement hardware, not an estimated model) on real handsets, breaking phone battery drain down by subsystem including cellular and Wi-Fi radio activity. Supplies the measured energy cost of keeping a radio link active, which is the concrete number behind any claim that continuous participation drains a phone's battery, as opposed to an unmeasured assertion that it does.

targets.title: Communication Latencies of Apple Push Notification Messages Relevant for Delivery of Time-Critical Information to Anesthesia Providers
targets.authors: Richard H. Epstein, Franklin Dexter, Brian Rothman
targets.why_needed: A four-month, 24-hour-a-day controlled measurement of Apple Push Notification Service delivery latency to real iOS devices over both Wi-Fi and cellular paths, sending one probe message per minute throughout. Reports mean latency under 100 seconds but a non-trivial fraction of days with at least one severely delayed delivery (up to 42% of days on the iPhone in this study's device sample). This is a primary-source measurement of the reliability of the push-based wake mechanism that a backgrounded phone depends on to be reachable at all, as opposed to the vendor's stated design intent for the service.

notes: Domain L had almost no coverage from the prior pass; that document's own text (not carried forward as a source of constraints, only mined for its one citable figure) named the 2025-26 DCUtR-in-IPFS study, so that paper anchors this list and everything else was built outward from it by forward/backward citation mining plus targeted search. IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO A FIGURE ALREADY IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOCUMENTS: prior-pass-corpus.md line 183 and line 191 state the DCUtR 70% figure as an unconditional hole-punching success rate. The published-version abstract (arXiv 2604.12484, which supersedes the October-2025 four-author preprint 2510.27500) states it explicitly as a CONDITIONAL success rate 'given that prerequisite relay reservation and public address discovery succeed' -- the earlier preprint's abstract omits that conditioning clause. A later pass extracting this paper's full text must determine what fraction of all connection attempts even reach that conditioned starting point, or the 70% figure will overstate end-to-end direct-connectivity odds. Two DOIs in this list (TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26's registered ACM DOI 10.1145/3777912.3809138, and note the arXiv-assigned DOI is what is actually recorded in the doi field above since the ACM one does not yet resolve) and the venue for BUCHET-CCR-25 should be re-checked at extraction time in case formal publication has completed. Two topics named in the assignment came back with no citable academic primary source despite an extended search: (1) large-scale independent measurement of WebRTC TURN-relay usage rates in production (every figure found -- 10-25%, 15-20%, 20%, 22%, 40-60%, 60-70% depending on deployment -- traces to vendor blog posts or unlabeled aggregate dashboards, never a paper whose methodology is inspectable, so none is included as a target; this is a genuine literature gap, not an oversight) and (2) a peer-reviewed measurement study of decentralized/P2P messaging apps specifically under iOS/Android background-execution suspension (searched under mobile background execution, Doze, background app refresh, and by the named apps Briar and Berty; nothing found beyond platform vendor documentation, which is a primary source for the constraint itself but not a measurement of an application under it). A later pass should try USENIX/MobiSys/SenSys full-text search directly rather than general web search for both gaps before concluding they do not exist. Epidemic-routing and delay-tolerant-networking literature (Vahdat/Becker, Fall's DTN architecture RFC 4838, PRoPHET, Pocket Switched Networks) was deliberately excluded after inspection: that literature solves intermittent radio-layer connectivity in physically disconnected mesh networks, a different problem from an internet-connected phone whose OS suspends its sockets while backgrounded, and including it would conflate the two failure modes. POST/ePost (Mislove et al., HotOS 2003) is the one included exception, kept because its replica-set store-and-forward design answers the actual question (relaying for a reachable-but-currently-absent recipient on the same internet) rather than the mesh-networking question. Symmetric-NAT prevalence in cellular networks specifically (a bimodal ~40% symmetric / ~20% full-cone split reported in secondary summaries) traces to Wang et al. SIGCOMM 2011 by methodology match, but the exact percentages have not been read from that paper's full text and must be verified, not assumed, at extraction time -- record them only if Wang et al. actually states them; if the paper's own numbers differ, the secondary summary is wrong and should be discarded per this project's rule 1. QRank and SwarmSearch (the two unresolved-identity items in the brief's open gaps) do not appear in this domain.
